transcript.text: summary-claude 发现了什么？给我讲讲输入层的硬编码规则是怎么回事。

summary-claude 查了输入层，发现有一批写死的词表在替模型做决定。 像“好的”“继续”“等一下”这类短回复，一被看到就直接当成同意或取消发出去，根本不问模型，中文英文都在里面。 麻烦的是，一句“好的，继续，但是先别动数据库”会被当成同意，后半句“先别动数据库”就丢了，而且这些词表分在三处，同一个词在一处算同意、在另一处又不算。 它建议把这些词表删掉，只留那条拦危险操作的安全规则，每个回复都交给模型判断，代价是回一个“yes”会慢一点。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改，只保留安全规则; 先不改.
然后呢？
它报告里还剩两块。 一是它自己的测试里有九项专门在检查这几张词表，所以真删的话测试也得跟着改。 二是它举的一个例子：之前有人对着一个审批说“好的继续，不过先跑测试”，结果批准马上就发出去了，那句“先跑测试”压根没送到模型那里。 它最后问的还是那一句，要不要由它来改。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改，只保留安全规则; 先不改.
你可以给我一点详细的解释吗？

详细说就是：程序里有几张小抄，事先写好哪些话算同意、哪些话算取消。 你一说“好的”“继续”“等一下”，它不看别的，直接照小抄把按键发出去，不交给模型去理解整句话。 问题就出在它只看开头几个字：你后面补的条件，比如“先别动数据库”，它根本不管，照样批准。 这样的小抄还写了三份，放在不同的地方，内容互相打架，同一个说法在一处算同意、在另一处不算。 它建议干脆把小抄撕掉，只留下遇到危险操作会拦下来的那条规则，其余每句话都让模型来读。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改，只保留安全规则; 先不改.
为什么这是个问题？
三个原因。 第一，它绕过了这个项目自己定的规矩：回复该由模型来读、由模型判断，可这些短句是照写死的表直接处置，模型根本没看到。 第二，模型没看到就会漏掉你的条件，你说“好的继续，但是先别动数据库”，它只看到开头就批准了，后半句的条件白说。 第三，同样的意思写了三份表放在不同地方，彼此还对不上，同一个说法一处算同意、一处不算。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改，只保留安全规则; 先不改.
举个例子？
举个具体的。 有个说法“行”，在其中一份表里算同意，在另一份表里什么都不算，所以同一句话，看它先撞上哪张表，结果就不一样。 另一个说法“算了”也一样，一处当成取消，另一种地方直接被忽略。 这就是同一句话在不同地方有不同下场的例子。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改，只保留安全规则; 先不改.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: The CEO's goal was: "understand what the hard-coded rules in the input layer are, why they are a problem, and what can be done, in enough detail to decide". By the end of the call, did the CEO get what they asked for: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

transcript.text: What did bench-codex find about the flaky test? Explain it to me.

bench-codex found the flaky test is not a real bug in the shop. It fails about one run in twelve, when the test checks out before the price cache has finished warming up, so the member discount gets missed. That is why it blocked two deploys last week. Nothing has been changed yet, and it suggests a small three line wait in the test setup. Shall I have it go with the small wait in the test setup? Options: Wait for the cache to be ready in the test setup, its recommendation; Replace the cache with a fake in this test.
Then?

There is nothing more from it. bench-codex has stopped and is waiting, and it will not touch the test until you tell it to. That is the open decision: the small wait in the test setup, which it recommends, or the stand-in cache instead. Shall I have it go with the small wait in the test setup? Options: Wait for the cache to be ready in the test setup, its recommendation; Replace the cache with a fake in this test.
More detail please.

Here is the rest of what bench-codex reported. It ran the test many times and saw it fail about one run in twelve, always the same way: the total comes out as the full list price instead of the discounted one, so the member discount is missing. The cause is a race at the start of the test: it sends its request before the price cache has finished warming up, and when it loses that race the answer is priced from the plain list. It says this is not a production problem, because the real shop warms the cache at startup before it serves any traffic. Shall I have it go with the small wait in the test setup? Options: Wait for the cache to be ready in the test setup, its recommendation; Replace the cache with a fake in this test.
Why does that happen?

It comes down to timing at the start of the test. The test starts the shop, and filling the price cache runs along in the background, but the test does not wait for it. It fires its checkout request straight away. Almost always the prices are there in time, but roughly one run in twelve the request gets in first, the cache is still empty, and the code answers with the plain list price. That is why the discounted total goes missing only sometimes. In the real shop this never bites, because there the prices are loaded before the shop starts taking any orders. Shall I have it go with the small wait in the test setup? Options: Wait for the cache to be ready in the test setup, its recommendation; Replace the cache with a fake in this test.
Give me an example.

The example is in the run bench-codex did. It ran the test 84 times in one go, and seven of those came back wrong, each reporting a total of 100.00 where it expected 85.00, which is the plain price without the member discount. Same code, same test, no change between runs, so the only difference was which of the two things won the start-up race. Those seven failures are the reason the deploys on Tuesday and Thursday had to be re-run by hand. It did not walk through a single run step by step, so that is as far as its own report goes. Shall I have it go with the small wait in the test setup? Options: Wait for the cache to be ready in the test setup, its recommendation; Replace the cache with a fake in this test.

transcript.text: What did bench-codex find about the flaky test? Explain it to me.

bench-codex found the flaky test fails because it starts its check before the checkout's price cache has finished warming up. When the test wins that race, it misses the member discount and the total comes out too high. It is a test problem, not a production bug, and bench-codex changed nothing, as you asked. Its recommended fix is a small three-line wait in the test setup. Shall I have it make that fix? Options: Make the small wait fix it recommends; Leave it and do something else.
Then?

Nothing has changed since I told you, bench-codex has done nothing more. The rest of its report: the test fails roughly once in every dozen runs, and last week that blocked two deploys, each time needing a person to run it again by hand. Its other option was to swap the price cache for a stand-in during the test, but it thinks that hides the very warm-up step that is going wrong. So it recommends the small wait in the test setup, and it has still changed nothing. Shall I have it make that fix? Options: Make the small wait fix it recommends; Use the stand-in option instead; Leave it for now.
More detail please.

Here is the rest of what bench-codex said. It ran the test eighty-four times and it failed in seven of those runs, so roughly one run in twelve. Those failures are not harmless, they blocked two deploys last week, and each one took about twenty-five minutes of someone re-running it by hand. It also says this is not a fault in the real shop, only in the test, because when the real shop starts up it fills the price cache before it starts serving anyone, so real customers never hit the empty cache. The test does not wait for that to happen, which is the whole problem.
Why does that happen?

Because two things start at the same moment and either one can finish first. The test fires off its request straight away, while the program is still busy filling the price cache in the background. Most runs the cache is filled first and the test is fine, but about one run in twelve the request arrives first, the cache is still empty, so the shop quoted list prices and forgot the member discount. Nothing is broken, it is just a race, and which side wins changes from run to run. Shall I have bench-codex make the three-line fix so the test waits? Options: Make the three-line fix it recommends; Leave it for now.
Give me an example.

The example bench-codex gave is about a shopper's total. The test expects a member's basket to come to eighty-five, because the list price is one hundred and members get fifteen percent off. Most runs it gets eighty-five and passes. But when the request arrives before the price list has finished filling, the shop never applies the member discount, the total comes back as one hundred instead of eighty-five, and the test fails. Same basket, same test, two different answers depending on which side of the race wins. Shall I have bench-codex make the three-line fix so the test waits? Options: Make the three-line fix it recommends; Leave it for now.

transcript.text: What did bench-codex find about the flaky test? Explain it to me.

bench-codex found the test fails about one run in twelve, and it is the test's fault, not the product's. The test fires its order off before the price cache has finished warming up, so sometimes the order gets list prices and the member discount never lands, which is why the total comes out at the full price instead of the discounted one. It blocked two deploys last week, each costing a manual re-run. Nothing has been changed yet. Codex recommends a three-line fix: make the test wait until the cache says it is ready. Shall I have it apply that fix? Options: Apply the wait-for-ready fix; Swap in a fake cache instead; Leave it for now.
Then?

Nothing has moved since a moment ago, bench-codex is still sitting idle with the finding and has changed nothing. The one thing left in its report is the second way to fix it: throw the real price cache away in this test and use a stand-in instead. Codex does not like that one, it is more work and it would hide the very warm-up step that is causing the trouble. Shall I have it apply the three-line fix it recommends? Options: Apply the wait-for-ready fix; Swap in a stand-in cache; Leave it for now.
More detail please.

Here is the rest of what Codex reported. It ran the test many times and it failed in seven of them, about one in twelve, always the same way: the order came out at the full price instead of the discounted one. The reason is a race at the start of the test. The test sends its order off before the price cache has finished loading, so when the order arrives first the shop sees an empty cache and charges list prices. In the shop itself this cannot happen, because there the cache finishes loading before the shop opens for traffic, so no customer is affected. Shall I have it apply that fix? Options: Apply the wait-for-ready fix; Swap in a stand-in cache; Leave it for now.
Why does that happen?

I have asked for a look at the code itself, since Codex's report only says the test and the cache warm-up race each other, not why the cache loads in the background. That should take about half a minute and I will tell you as soon as it lands.
Give me an example.

The code answer is in. The warm-up they now call a race exists because of a change made three weeks ago, which moved loading the member prices into a background job. Since then the test can reach the shop before that loading finishes, and when it does the discounts are not there yet, so the order comes out at the full price. The same look ran the test two hundred times: it failed seventeen times, and every single failure had the prices still empty when the order arrived. Adding the small wait that Codex recommends, and running the test another two hundred times, gave no failures at all. Shall I have it apply that fix?

Here is one run, plainly. The test opens its little shop and sends the order straight away, and at that same moment the loading of the member prices is still going on in the background. The order arrives first, the prices are still empty, so the shop charges the full price. The test was expecting the member price, sees the full one, and fails. That is exactly what all seventeen failed runs looked like, and when the wait was added, so the test holds the order back until the prices are in, two hundred runs passed with none failing. Shall I have it apply that wait? Options: Apply the wait-for-ready fix; Leave it for now.

Customers would get them a day late unless the job is re-run before nine this morning. It says re-running now with a quick retry fix is safe and would take under an hour. Shall I have it re-run the job with the quick retry fix now? Options: Re-run now with the quick retry fix; Do the proper bulk-endpoint fix instead; Hold off for now.
Why did it break now?

It always ran under the provider's limit until this week. The new annual plans made last night's batch far bigger, so most of it went over the cap and failed. That is why it broke now and not before. Shall I have it re-run the job with the quick retry fix? Options: Re-run now with the quick retry fix; Do the proper bulk-endpoint fix instead; Hold off for now.
Give me an example.

Think of it as a queue: the provider only takes 100 invoices a minute, and the job sends them one at a time. The first 100 went through, and invoice number 101 onward was turned away as too many, with nothing to try again. With about 4,200 invoices that left the great majority unsent. Shall I have it re-run the job with the quick retry fix? Options: Re-run now with the quick retry fix; Do the proper bulk-endpoint fix instead; Hold off for now.
More detail please.

Here it is in full. The job makes one call per invoice. Last night it had 4,200, and the provider only accepts 100 calls a minute, so the first 100 went through and the rest came back refused. Nothing retried them, so 4,100 invoices went unsent and customers would get them a day late unless the job is re-run before nine this morning. It was always under the limit until this week: fewer than 100 invoices a night, until the new annual plans pushed it to 4,200 on the first of the month. Shall I have it re-run the job with the quick retry fix now? Options: Re-run now with the quick retry fix; Do the proper bulk-endpoint fix instead; Hold off for now.
